questions.q: What is the real skill this lesson teaches, underneath the Driftwood example?
options: Writing Azure CLI scripts
Requirements clarification — turning a vague ask into a specific, answerable scope
Choosing a VM size family
Configuring a Network Security Group
questions.explain: This lesson is entirely about turning "migrate it to Azure" into a specific, written scope before any Azure resource gets touched.

questions.q: In the clarified scope, what exactly makes up "the workload" Theo needs to migrate?
options: Every application Driftwood runs, on-prem and in the cloud
Only the product images, since the server itself is staying on-prem
The product-catalog app's static product images plus the application server that serves the catalog pages
A brand-new application Theo needs to write from scratch
questions.explain: Priya's ask, once clarified, covers two concrete pieces: the static product images and the application server itself — not a rewrite and not the whole company's app portfolio.

questions.q: Why does the deadline matter as part of the scope, not just a date on a calendar?
options: It doesn't — deadlines are a project-management detail, not part of scoping
Priya wants the migration validated at least a week before launch, which shapes how much time there is for testing and fixing problems
Azure resources can only be created on specific dates
The deadline determines which Azure region is available
questions.explain: Clarifying "before launch" into a concrete date, with a validation buffer, is exactly the kind of hidden detail that changes how the whole project gets planned.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly NOT something Theo should decide during this first conversation with Priya?
options: What the actual deadline is
Whether Priya wants to review the plan before anything is built
Which specific Azure services best fit the migration
What "done" looks like for this project
questions.explain: Picking specific Azure services is next lesson's job. This conversation is about scope and deadline, not architecture.

questions.q: What makes a scope statement "specific enough," according to this lesson?
options: You could hand it to a teammate and they'd understand exactly what "done" looks like
It names every Azure service that might be used
It avoids mentioning the stakeholder by name
It is written in formal project-management language
questions.explain: The lesson's test for a specific scope is whether a teammate, given only that sentence, would understand the same finish line you have in mind.
